summary: Teach 'a half' as ONE OF TWO EQUAL parts of a whole, where the equality — not merely having two pieces — is the defining idea. Build on children's informal fair-sharing intuition, starting by sharing a set of objects evenly between two before partitioning a single object. Cover halving of single objects (fold/cut a shape), lengths (split a strip at the midpoint), and quantities/sets (share counters into two equal groups). Reinforce that two halves recompose the whole, and that 'half of' a quantity is found by sharing equally into two. For ages 5–6.
misconceptions: Any two pieces count as 'halves' regardless of size — the equal-parts requirement is missing
A half is only the one piece you take, not seeing that both parts are halves and together make the whole
Calling any fractional part 'a half' (a documented early error — IES)
Sharing a set by equal NUMBER of items rather than equal AMOUNT when items differ in size (number-vs-quantity confusion)

activities.title: The halving bench: make it fair
steps: Drag a cutting line across a rectangular chocolate bar (cutting straight across its length); when the cut is off-centre, note that the two parts are unequal (e.g. they glow red / are labelled 'not halves – not fair') and when at the midpoint the two parts are equal (snap green / labelled 'two equal halves').
Slide the two equal halves back together to remake the whole bar, saying 'two halves make one whole'.
Switch to a set mode: share a plate of biscuits (or counters) into two hoops, and only accept it as 'done' when the two amounts match.
Check equality by matching or overlaying the parts, and describe each as 'a half' and 'the other half'.
activities.insight: A half requires two EQUAL parts; the count of two pieces alone does not make halves. Both parts are halves, and together they rebuild the whole.

activities.title: Share the set first
steps: Share a set of objects (for example, 8 counters, or 6 sweets) evenly between two people, giving one each in turn until the pile is gone.
State how many each person gets and, when all the objects are the same size, that each group is 'half of' the set.
With objects of different sizes (big and small sweets), check whether equal COUNT gives equal AMOUNT, and discuss which sharing is fair.
activities.insight: 'Half of' a quantity is found by sharing equally into two groups; fairness means equal amount, which may differ from equal number when items vary in size.

activities.title: Halved or not? Sort and choose
steps: Sort pictures of shapes and sets into 'halved' (two equal parts) versus 'not halved' (unequal parts).
Choose which picture shows a half when one option has an unequal cut as a tempting wrong choice.
For each 'not halved' example, say what is wrong and what would make it a half.
activities.insight: Recognising halves means checking for two EQUAL parts, so an unequal split is not halves even though it has two pieces.

activities.title: Reference display: name the parts
steps: Tap or point to each half of a halved object to highlight it, then name it 'a half' and 'the other half'.
Read or say 'two halves make one whole' while watching the parts combine.
activities.insight: Both parts of a fairly divided whole are halves, and the two halves together make one whole.

checkQuestion: Show a chocolate bar snapped into two pieces - one big, one small. Ask: 'Is one of these pieces a half of the bar? How do you know?' Then ask: 'What would I have to do to make two halves - and if I put the two halves back together, what do I get?'
checkAnswer: No - the two pieces are not equal, so neither is a half. Halves must be two EQUAL parts; you would have to break the bar so both pieces are the same size. Two equal halves put back together make the whole bar.
